title: CDC in Uganda - Centers for Disease Control and Prevention | CDC (.gov)

analysis.time: The CDC's report on the Ebola outbreak in Uganda was published on August 20, 2026. The outbreak was reported to have ended in 87 days, with the last case likely occurring in late June 2026.
analysis.location_and_population: The outbreak occurred in Uganda, specifically in the border districts and points of entry where CDC has been supporting disease surveillance since 2018. The affected population included individuals in these regions, with a focus on those at risk of exposure to the Sudan virus.
analysis.event: An Ebola outbreak was reported in Uganda, with 14 confirmed cases and 4 deaths. The CDC collaborated with the Ministry of Health (MOH) and local partners to contain the outbreak, which was successfully managed within 90 days with no cross-border spread. The outbreak was caused by the Sudan virus, which is a related entity under the topic contract.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: The outbreak reported 14 cases and 4 deaths, with no cross-border spread. The overall risk to the American public and travelers remains low, as no cases of Ebola disease have been confirmed in the United States due to the outbreak. The CDC supported outbreak response efforts, including containment and surveillance.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The CDC and its partners supported the Ministry of Health in containing the outbreak, which was successfully managed within 90 days. The outbreak ended in 87 days, and all ten treated patients survived. The CDC also provided technical support for outbreak investigations and response, including strengthening laboratory systems and workforce capacity.

analysis.brief_en: The CDC in Uganda reported an Ebola outbreak caused by the Sudan virus, which was contained within 90 days with no cross-border spread. The outbreak resulted in 14 confirmed cases and 4 deaths, and all ten treated patients survived, marking Uganda's highest survival rate to date. The CDC collaborated with the Ministry of Health (MOH) and local partners to manage the outbreak, including strengthening laboratory systems and workforce capacity. The overall risk to the American public and travelers remains low, as no cases of Ebola disease have been confirmed in the United States due to this outbreak. The CDC has been actively involved in disease surveillance and emergency response in Uganda since 2018, supporting efforts to detect and contain outbreaks such as Ebola, monkeypox, and cholera.

The outbreak resulted in 14 confirmed cases and 4 deaths, and all ten treated patients survived, marking Uganda's highest survival rate to date. The overall risk to the American public and travelers remains low, as no cases of Ebola disease have been confirmed in the United States due to this outbreak. title: From outbreak response to resilience - UNICEF

analysis.time: During the Marburg Virus Disease (MVD) outbreak in early 2025, and today (2026-08-20) with the implementation of the upgraded water system.
analysis.location_and_population: Biharamulo District Hospital, United Republic of Tanzania, serving a population of 45 health workers, 168 beds, hundreds of patients and caregivers, and an average of 205 deliveries each month.
analysis.event: The Marburg Virus Disease (MVD) outbreak in early 2025 highlighted the critical need for reliable water access at Biharamulo District Hospital, which was previously limited to three days per week. The hospital implemented a water system upgrade with support from UNICEF and the Republic of Korea to improve infection prevention and control.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: The hospital had limited water storage capacity (18,000 litres) and faced challenges in maintaining hygiene standards during the outbreak. The upgraded system now provides reliable water access, supporting infection prevention and control, environmental cleaning, and patient care.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The upgraded water system has been implemented, and reliable water is now available throughout the hospital. The system was funded by the Republic of Korea through UNICEF and supported by the Government of Tanzania and SAWA.

analysis.brief_en: This news report highlights the challenges faced by Biharamulo District Hospital in Tanzania during the Marburg Virus Disease (MVD) outbreak in early 2025. At the time, the hospital had an unreliable water supply, available only three days per week, which hindered critical hygiene practices such as handwashing and surface cleaning. Nurse Aloysia Emmanuel Bakuza emphasized the importance of water in preventing infections during the outbreak. To address this, UNICEF, with funding from the Republic of Korea, partnered with the Tanzanian government and SAWA to improve water, sanitation, and hygiene services. The project included drilling a borehole, installing a high-capacity pump, and constructing a 50,000-litre water storage tank. These upgrades have ensured reliable water access, supporting infection prevention and control, environmental cleaning, and patient care. The improved system has enhanced the hospital's resilience and preparedness for future health emergencies.
analysis.summary_en: This news report highlights the challenges faced by Biharamulo District Hospital in Tanzania during the Marburg Virus Disease (MVD) outbreak in early 2025. At the time, the hospital had an unreliable water supply, available only three days per week, which hindered critical hygiene practices such as handwashing and surface cleaning. Nurse Aloysia Emmanuel Bakuza emphasized the importance of water in preventing infections during the outbreak. To address this, UNICEF, with funding from the Republic of Korea, partnered with the Tanzanian government and SAWA to improve water, sanitation, and hygiene services. The project included drilling a borehole, installing a high-capacity pump, and constructing a 50,000-litre water storage tank. These upgrades have ensured reliable water access, supporting infection prevention and control, environmental cleaning, and patient care. The improved system has enhanced the hospital's resilience and preparedness for future health emergencies.
